claims.claim: Cycle Toronto and two individual applicants announced Oct. 13 they will seek leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada over Ontario's bike lane removal law.
claims.attributed_to: Cycle Toronto; The Canadian Press; Globe and Mail

claims.claim: The applicants are represented by Ecojustice and Paliare Roland Rosenberg Rothstein LLP; co-applicants are Eva Stanger-Ross and Narada Kiondo.
The Ontario Court of Appeal's August ruling overturned a lower-court decision that found the removal plan an unconstitutional risk to cyclist safety under Section 7 of the Charter.
claims.attributed_to: The Canadian Press; Globe and Mail

claims.claim: The Supreme Court has not agreed to hear the appeal.
Whether the leave application has been formally filed is not established, as of Oct. 15.
A 2024 provincial law empowers Ontario to remove about 19 km of protected bike lanes on Bloor, Yonge and University.
claims.attributed_to: The Canadian Press; Globe and Mail

claims.claim: Ontario says removing bike lanes and restoring car lanes will cut congestion, which it says costs the provincial economy $56 billion a year.
claims.attributed_to: Dakota Brasier, spokesman for Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria

claims.claim: A government-commissioned report found the removals could increase collisions by 54 per cent among all road users without meaningfully reducing congestion.
Work to remove a 1.2-km section of Bloor Street West between Clissold Road and Royal York Road was slated for the night of Oct. 13.
The work was halted when pylon trucks were blocked by protesters; Sarkaria posted on X that the bike lanes 'are coming out.'
The Supreme Court generally takes several months to decide whether to hear an appeal, too late to affect the immediate Bloor removal plans.
Toronto's mayoral election is about two weeks away, with the two front-runners holding opposing bike-lane positions.
Etobicoke Bloor Street West bike lane removal resumed Wednesday afternoon and is underway, with crews removing pavement markings, signs and concrete barriers.
claims.attributed_to: CBC News; TorontoToday; Humber Et Cetera

claims.claim: The work covers roughly one kilometre of Bloor Street West from Clissold Road to Royal York Road, starting west of Islington Avenue.
The removal will require temporary vehicle lane reductions and is expected to finish in November.
Two people were arrested during Wednesday's protest.
Nina Thi Thi Tran, 25, of Hamilton was charged with obstructing a peace officer and mischief under $5,000 after refusing to move from a curb barrier.
claims.attributed_to: Toronto police, via CBC News and CityNews

claims.claim: A second person was arrested near Bloor West and Islington Avenue for mischief; charges were not stated as of Wednesday night.
Pylon trucks were blocked by protesters Tuesday night and escorted off Bloor Street shortly before 8 p.m.
Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria said on X the work was 'halted by protesters' and that the bike lanes 'are coming out.'
Toronto Police Chief Myron Demkiw said there is no injunction preventing the removal and that obstructing the lawful work carries potential criminal liability.
claims.attributed_to: Myron Demkiw, via CityNews and TorontoToday

claims.claim: The mayor's spokesperson said the work proceeded despite city proposals to keep bike lanes while restoring a traffic lane, a compromise already used further west on Bloor.
No City of Toronto news release or media advisory on the bike lane removal appears in the city's media room list through Oct. 13.
The Supreme Court has not agreed to hear the appeal, and the leave announcement does not suspend the work.
Crews resumed removing the Etobicoke Bloor Street West bike lanes Wednesday afternoon, stripping pavement markings, signs and concrete barriers.
